section.title: Mordecai Honored
section.sectionRationale: This is the fulcrum of the whole book, the night everything turns. The king cannot sleep, calls for the royal chronicles, and hears, by no plan of his own, that Mordecai once saved his life and was never rewarded. At that very moment Haman arrives to request Mordecai's execution. Before he can speak, the king asks how to honor a man he delights in; Haman, sure it is himself, describes a lavish public parade, and is ordered to lead Mordecai through the city in it. Haman goes home humiliated, and even his wife and advisers see his doom approaching.
section.thesis: Without a miracle or a spoken word from heaven, a hidden God rules a sleepless night, an open book, and a proud man's assumption to exalt the faithful and abase the arrogant, the great reversal on which the story pivots.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the sleepless night and the forgotten record; Haman trapped by his own pride into honoring Mordecai; and Mordecai paraded while Haman is humiliated and warned of his fall.

units.label: A sleepless night, a forgotten record

verses.text: That night {{shenah|sleep}} escaped the king; so he ordered the Book of Records, the Chronicles, to be brought in and read to him.
And there it was found recorded that Mordecai had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the eunuchs who guarded the king’s entrance, when they had conspired to assassinate King Xerxes.
The king inquired, “What honor or dignity has been bestowed on Mordecai for this act?” “Nothing has been done for him,” replied the king’s attendants.

units.label: Haman trapped by his own pride
units.note: the honor he plans for himself falls to Mordecai

verses.text: “Who is in the court?” the king asked. Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the palace to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared for him.
So the king’s attendants answered him, “Haman is there, standing in the court.” “Bring him in,” ordered the king.

Haman entered, and the king asked him, “What should be done for the man whom the king is delighted to {{yaqar|honor}}?” Now Haman thought to himself, “Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?”
And Haman told the king, “For the man whom the king is delighted to honor,
have them bring a royal robe that the king himself has worn and a horse on which the king himself has ridden, one with a royal crest placed on its head.

Let the robe and the horse be entrusted to one of the king’s most noble princes. Let them array the man the king wants to honor and parade him on the horse through the city square, proclaiming before him, ‘This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!’”
“Hurry,” said the king to Haman, “and do just as you proposed. Take the robe and the horse to Mordecai the Jew, who is sitting at the king’s gate. Do not neglect anything that you have suggested.”

units.label: Mordecai paraded, Haman humiliated
units.note: his own household foresees his fall

verses.text: So Haman took the robe and the horse, arrayed Mordecai, and paraded him through the city square, crying out before him, “This is what is done for the man whom the king is delighted to honor!”
Then Mordecai returned to the king’s gate. But Haman rushed home, with his head covered in grief.

Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened. His advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, “Since Mordecai, before whom your downfall has begun, is Jewish, you will not prevail against him, for surely you will {{naphal|fall}} before him.”
While they were still speaking with Haman, the king’s eunuchs arrived and rushed him to the banquet that Esther had prepared.

shenah.gloss: Sleep. The verse reads literally that the king's sleep fled, an ordinary insomnia with no stated cause. In a book where God is never named, this small, everyday event is the hinge on which the whole rescue turns; Scripture elsewhere insists the king's heart, and even his sleeplessness, is in the LORD's hand.

yaqar.gloss: Honor, that which is precious or prized. The refrain the man whom the king is delighted to honor rings through the scene with heavy irony, as Haman plans for himself the very glory that falls to Mordecai. The word threads the great reversal: the proud are stripped of the honor they crave, and the faithful are lifted up.

naphal.gloss: To fall, be brought down, be defeated. Haman's own wife and advisers use it twice: his downfall has begun, and he will surely fall. On the lips of pagans it sounds almost like an oracle, and the narrative treats it as sure, for the arrogant are already falling before the faithful whom the hidden God defends.

basic.context: This is the turning point of the book, and it happens without a single miracle. The king cannot sleep, so he has the royal records read to him, and hears that Mordecai once foiled an assassination plot and was never rewarded. Just then Haman arrives, planning to ask permission to hang Mordecai. Before he can, the king asks how best to honor a man he delights in. Haman, certain it must be himself, describes an extravagant public parade in royal robes on a royal horse. The king says: excellent, now do all of that for Mordecai the Jew. Haman must lead his enemy through the city, proclaiming his honor, then slinks home in disgrace, where even his wife and friends tell him he is doomed.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter is a masterpiece of irony, and its central question is: who is running this? There is no voice from heaven, no visible act of God, only a sleepless king, a well-timed reading, and a proud man's fatal assumption. Yet the coincidences pile up until the reader cannot miss the hidden hand. The key questions are whether these events are chance or providence, and what Zeresh's grim prediction reveals. The abiding lesson is that God governs the smallest, most ordinary details to exalt the humble and bring down the proud.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter hinges on the king's fled sleep, shenah, an ordinary insomnia that Scripture elsewhere says is in the LORD's hand. It rings with the refrain of honor, yaqar, the precious glory Haman craves for himself and is forced to bestow on Mordecai. And it ends with the word fall, naphal, spoken twice by Haman's own household as they foresee his ruin. Three plain words carry the whole reversal.
basic.typology: Mordecai, the faithful servant whose good deed went unrewarded and who was marked for death, is suddenly clothed in royal honor. He foreshadows Christ, who humbled Himself, was rejected and condemned, and was then exalted by God. The proud Haman brought low and the lowly Mordecai raised is the very shape of the gospel: God exalts the humble and humbles the proud.
basic.christ: The great reversal here points straight to Christ. The one destined for the gallows is paraded in royal robes; the humble servant is exalted while the proud enemy is abased. So it is with Jesus, who took the lowest place, was numbered with the condemned, and was then highly exalted and given the name above every name. The parade of Mordecai in borrowed royal glory is a faint picture of the resurrection triumph of the true faithful Servant.
basic.god: God is not named, and no miracle occurs, yet this is the most obviously God-governed chapter in the book. A king's insomnia, the choice of which record to read, the exact moment of Haman's arrival, all of it converges with a precision no accident could explain. The book is teaching us to see providence in the ordinary: the God who rules a sleepless night is ruling every detail of our lives too, and He does not forget His faithful servants.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 21 says the king's heart is a stream of water in the LORD's hand. First Samuel 2 declares that the LORD brings low and lifts up. Luke 1 sings that God scatters the proud and exalts the humble. And Philippians 2 shows Christ humbled to death and then exalted above all.
basic.oneStory: On a sleepless night, with no miracle and no spoken word, a hidden God overturns everything: the proud man is forced to honor the servant he meant to hang. It is the gospel reversal in miniature, the humbling of the arrogant and the exalting of the faithful, fulfilled when God raised the crucified Christ to the highest place.

context.literary:
Chapter 6 is the shortest route between two banquets and the hinge of the book's structure. Readers have long noticed that the story is built as a mirror. The rise of Haman, the decree and the fast lead to this night, and after it the scenes run in reverse: Haman's fall, the counter decree, the Jews' victory. Everything before chapter 6 tightens the noose; everything after loosens it. The turn comes on a single night, and it is signalled in the first words, 'that night'. Note that it is the very night after Haman built the gallows, so the narrator has placed the sleepless king and the ready gallows in the same evening.

The chapter is a small masterpiece of dramatic irony. The reader knows Haman has come to ask for Mordecai's death, verse 4, and the king does not. The king asks a question, and Haman hears in it the answer he has always wanted. The narrator lets Haman think it aloud, verse 6, and then lets him build a detailed picture of his own glory, verses 7 to 9, which the king turns into a command in one sentence, verse 10. The speech that Haman writes for his own honour is used word for word for his enemy. The phrase 'the man whom the king delights to honour' comes back four times, and the last time it is shouted in the street by Haman himself, verse 11.

The last section has the tightest turn of all. Haman covers his head in grief and runs home, and while his wife and friends are still speaking the king's eunuchs arrive to hurry him to the next banquet, verses 12 to 14. He is not given time to think. The chapter ends mid-stride, and the next scene, Esther 7, is already under way.
context.historical:
The Persian court kept written records, and its officials read them aloud. Ezra 4:15 and 6:1 and 2 show kings searching the archives for matters of state, and Esther 2:23 tells us the account of the plot against Xerxes was written down 'in the presence of the king'. Greek historians report that Persian kings kept a register of their 'benefactors' and rewarded them, so the king's question in verse 3, 'What honour has been given to Mordecai?', is exactly the kind of thing a Persian ruler would ask. It would have been a matter of some embarrassment to the king to find that a loyal man had gone unrewarded. Having a servant read aloud is a natural remedy for a restless mind, though the narrator makes it look less like a habit than an appointment.

The honours Haman proposes are royal in the extreme. A robe the king himself has worn, a horse he has ridden, and a crest on the horse's head all treat the honoured man as the king's double. In the ancient world the king's garments carried his presence. Haman's list therefore reveals an ambition that goes beyond gratitude toward a wish for a share of royal standing, and the king's later suspicion in Esther 7:8 fits with that. The parade is to be led by one of the highest nobles, through the city square, with a herald. It mirrors what Pharaoh did for Joseph, who was set in the second chariot with men calling before him, Genesis 41:42 and 43.

The reaction of Haman's household also has historical texture. Zeresh and the counsellors speak of the Jews as a people with a history, and they say that Haman will not prevail against them. Persians had seen Babylon fall and the exiles return under Cyrus, and Jewish resilience could have been common knowledge in Susa. It is striking that the wise men of Haman's court are the first to confess what the Jews' own people have not yet seen.
context.canonical:
The night of no sleep is a biblical device. Pharaoh's spirit was troubled and he summoned the wise men of Egypt, Genesis 41:8. Nebuchadnezzar had dreams that troubled his spirit and 'sleep escaped him', Daniel 2:1, and Darius spent a night fasting when 'sleep fled from him' after he had thrown Daniel to the lions, Daniel 6:18. In all three, a sleepless king becomes the doorway to God's servant being lifted up. Psalm 127:2 says that God gives sleep to His beloved; here He takes it from the powerful, and the point is the same, that rest and unrest are in His hand.

The parade repeats the story of Joseph, who was clothed in fine linen and made to ride in the second chariot while men called out before him, Genesis 41:42 and 43. In both stories a foreigner in a pagan court is publicly raised and the honour comes after long neglect. The wider pattern is announced in Hannah's song: 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes', 1 Samuel 2:8. Psalm 75:6 and 7 says it more plainly: 'it is God who judges; He brings down one and exalts another.' The reversal of Esther 6 is the plot of those verses in a single day.

The New Testament makes this into a principle. Jesus says, 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted', Luke 14:11 and Luke 18:14, and Mary sings that God has 'brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble', Luke 1:52. Paul finds the pattern fulfilled in Christ, who humbled Himself to the point of death and was highly exalted, Philippians 2:8 and 9. Finally, Zeresh's words about the Jews recall God's word to Abraham, 'whoever curses you I will curse', Genesis 12:3, a promise now spoken back by an enemy.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants the readers to feel the ordinary unfolding of events until the truth breaks in. Nothing in the chapter is a miracle. A king cannot sleep, an official reads the wrong scroll, or perhaps the right one, and a courtier arrives early. Every event is one that could happen on any night in any palace. Yet the author places them in a sequence so exact that no one can miss the point that someone is directing them.

He wants the readers to take that as encouragement. They are a small, scattered people under a decree, and it looks as if all the power belongs to others. The story tells them that the king's sleep, his reading and his conversation are not outside God's rule. He also wants them to learn from Mordecai, who does not campaign for his reward or complain that he was overlooked. He goes back to the gate, verse 12, and the honour comes from another direction. The author trusts that his readers will draw from this the conviction that faithful service is never wasted, even when it is forgotten for years.

And he wants them to see what pride does to a person's judgment. Haman's cleverness is undone by his self-regard, and the verse where he asks himself 'whom would the king delight to honour more than me?' becomes the trap. The story invites the reader to laugh, and then to tremble.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter narrates a series of events and offers no command. It does not say that kings will always be restless when justice is due, or that faithful service will always be rewarded in this life. Many people who saved others were never honoured. The story shows one occasion when God overturned a plan, and it does not promise the same timing to every believer.

The lessons that carry forward are about attitude. Mordecai's quiet return to duty models service that does not depend on being noticed, and it reflects Jesus' teaching that the humble will be exalted, though He does not say when. Haman's fall warns against the assumption that praise is always meant for us. It is also a caution against reading history as if every reversal were a direct message. The chapter invites trust in God's governing hand without turning that trust into a formula for predicting outcomes.

debates.question: Is the king's sleepless night chance or providence?

views.label: Providence
views.case: The events line up too neatly to be an accident. The king cannot sleep on this night, chooses this book and comes to this passage, and Haman arrives at the very moment he is asked about honour. Proverbs says that the lot is cast, but every decision is from the LORD, Proverbs 16:33, and the story reads as an illustration of that. Most Christian readers, and many Jewish ones, take the book as a deliberate portrait of hidden providence.

views.label: Narrative coincidence used to show irony
views.case: Others emphasise the literary skill of the book. It is a story, and stories are built with timing, so the events show the author's craft as much as God's hand. On this view the coincidence is meant to be felt as improbable, so that readers ask who is behind it, but the book does not itself assert a divine cause.

debates.bearing: The book asks the question without answering it, and the rest of Scripture provides the answer. A reader who holds that God governs all things will see the night as His doing, without having to claim that He is named in the text.

debates.question: Do Haman's proposed honours show that he wanted the throne?

views.label: Yes, a grasp at royal status
views.case: A robe the king has worn, a horse the king has ridden and a royal crest are the marks of kingship, and Haman is already the second man in the empire. His assumption that the king would honour 'me' shows how far his sense of entitlement has grown, and it may be why the king is quickly alarmed in Esther 7:8.

views.label: No, an extravagant courtier's fantasy
views.case: Others read the list as the dream of a man who wants public honour and nothing more. The king himself approves it without hesitation and applies it to Mordecai, which suggests that such honours could be granted by the king without implying a claim on his crown.

debates.bearing: Either way the list reveals what Haman most wanted, to be seen and admired. That is enough to explain the irony, and the story does not need to decide whether he wanted the throne.

study.originalLanguages:
The Hebrew of this chapter holds several small treasures beyond the words the study has already noticed.

The verb for the king's sleeplessness in verse 1 is nadad, whose usual sense is to flee or to wander. It is the word used for a bird that flits away, Proverbs 27:8, and here it is sleep that has flown. The text says that 'the king's sleep fled', as if sleep itself were a creature that had left the palace. The author does not say who sent it away, and that is part of the point.

The book the king asks for is the 'book of records of the chronicles', and the first of those nouns comes from the root for remembering. It is literally a book of memorials. That is a striking choice, because remembering is one of the book's chief threads. Haman is an Agagite, and God's own word about Amalek was that He would blot out their memory from under heaven, Exodus 17:14 and Deuteronomy 25:19. In this chapter it is Mordecai's deed that is remembered, in the king's own book, and Haman who is about to be forgotten.

The king says that the honoured man is one in whom the king 'delights', chafets, and Haman repeats the word again and again. It is the word for a desire that has settled on someone, used of the LORD who 'delights in loving devotion', Micah 7:18. Haman is taken in by it, since he assumes the delight is his, and the reader sees it fall on Mordecai instead.

When Haman rushes home, the text says his head was 'covered', a gesture of mourning and shame. David walked up the Mount of Olives with his head covered as he fled Absalom, 2 Samuel 15:30, and the same gesture appears in times of drought and disaster, Jeremiah 14:3. Haman is now dressed for the funeral that the story is preparing for him.

Finally, Zeresh says that Haman is falling before 'the seed of the Jews', and the Hebrew is the ordinary word for offspring, the same word used in the promise of Genesis 3:15 and 22:18. She may not intend the echo, but the reader who knows the Bible does.

typology.type: Mordecai, faithful and forgotten, then lifted up in a public procession
typology.fulfillment: A servant whose good deed goes unrewarded and who is marked for death is suddenly clothed in royal honour before the city. It foreshadows the pattern of Christ, who was despised and rejected and then exalted, Philippians 2:8 and 9. The escalation is in the scale: Mordecai receives a robe and a ride for a day, while Christ is given 'the name above all names' and the whole creation bows, Philippians 2:10. The type falls short because Mordecai's exaltation is temporary and dependent on a king's favour, and it came without any suffering that saved others.

typology.type: Haman leading his enemy through the streets
typology.fulfillment: The one who plotted the humiliation of another becomes the herald of that person's honour. It resembles the day when every knee will bow to the one the powers rejected, and every tongue will confess, Philippians 2:10 and 11. The proud, who wanted the honour for themselves, will one day give it to the one they refused. The type falls short because Haman's homage is forced and bitter, and he does not repent, while the confession before Christ will in some cases be glad and in some compelled.

typology.type: The book of records opened at the right page
typology.fulfillment: A record of a good deed long forgotten by people turns out to be remembered. It anticipates the books that will be opened at the last day, Revelation 20:12, and the assurance that God does not forget the work and love of His people, Hebrews 6:10. The escalation is that God's memory is perfect and His reward is sure, whereas the king's memory needed a sleepless night. The type falls short because the king's archive shows only what was seen, while God knows what was done in secret, Matthew 6:4.

typology.type: The robe and the horse given to the lowly
typology.fulfillment: The gift of royal robes to a man who had worn sackcloth in chapter 4 is a small picture of the exchange that God makes with His people, giving 'a garment of praise for a spirit of despair', Isaiah 61:3, and clothing them with garments of salvation, Isaiah 61:10. In Christ this becomes the robe of righteousness that covers the believer, Galatians 3:27. The type falls short because Mordecai's robe was borrowed for a day, and a believer's is permanent.

study.christ:
Esther 6 does not mention the Messiah, yet the shape of its central reversal is the shape of the gospel, and the New Testament says so in its own words.

The chapter shows a righteous servant honoured after being condemned. Mordecai has done good and been overlooked. He is marked for death on the gallows that stands ready. Then in the space of a day he is lifted up in public. The apostle Paul tells the story of Jesus in the same order: He humbled Himself, became obedient to death on a cross, and 'therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names', Philippians 2:8 and 9. What Esther 6 offers in a day, the gospel offers at the resurrection. The public that watched Jesus die watched Him die as a criminal, but God turned that verdict upside down, Acts 2:23 and 24. The difference is that Jesus was not honoured for a good deed forgotten by a king. He was raised by the Father because He had accomplished the redemption of His people.

The chapter also shows the proud made to serve the humble. Haman must shout Mordecai's praise in the street. The picture is a small anticipation of the day when 'every knee will bow', Philippians 2:10, including the knees of those who once refused. Haman's homage is not repentance, and it is a warning. Jesus said that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, Luke 14:11, and He taught that in His own life. Unlike Haman, He never grasped at honour, Philippians 2:6.

The third link is the picture of a king who is read to in the night and finds that a debt of gratitude is unpaid. The New Testament says that God is not unjust to forget the work and love shown to His name, Hebrews 6:10. The debt God owes to His Son is greater, and He pays it in glory. In the same way the debt He owes to His people who served in secret is a debt of grace that He will honour, Matthew 6:4.

As always, a caution. Mordecai is not the Messiah; he is a faithful man who does his duty and is honoured for it. The chapter's parallels to Christ are of pattern, not of prophecy, and its details, such as the colour of the robe or the type of horse, carry no coded meaning. The great continuity is the truth that God brings down the proud and lifts the humble, and that this reaches its fullest form in Jesus, whose exaltation is the pledge of every believer's.
study.god:
Esther 6 is the book's clearest picture of God at work without being named, and it teaches several things about Him.

God rules the smallest things. Nothing in the chapter is spectacular. It is a night, a book and a question, and yet the whole future of a people turns on them. The Bible says that 'the king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD', Proverbs 21:1, and that no plan can stand against Him, Proverbs 21:30. The doctrine of providence is not confined to great events. It extends to a restless night and to who is standing in the outer court at dawn. Jesus taught the same thing when He said that not a sparrow falls without the Father, Matthew 10:29.

God remembers. The king's book is the visible record, but the reader is meant to sense a greater Memory behind it. God 'heard their groaning and remembered His covenant', Exodus 2:24, and He is the One who does not forget the labour of love, Hebrews 6:10. The chapter turns the ordinary act of reading old records into a picture of a God who keeps accounts and pays them at the right time, not before.

God resists the proud and honours the humble. This is stated as a principle in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 and 6, and here it is dramatised. Haman is undone by his own words, in a way that no visible punishment could improve on. The chapter also teaches that God's justice is patient. Mordecai was not rewarded for years, and no one in the story was troubled by it, yet the debt was noted.

God's ways are hidden but not absent. The narrator does not speak of Him, and Mordecai never mentions Him in the chapter. A believing reader sees Him in everything, and an unbelieving reader could see only coincidence. The book leaves room for both, and in doing so it teaches something about the kind of faith God asks of His people in times when He is not obvious. Isaiah says of Him, 'Truly You are a God who hides Himself', Isaiah 45:15, and the book of Esther is a narrative of that verse.

For worship, the chapter calls for gratitude for ordinary things: a night's sleep, a timely word, an answer that arrives before the question is asked. It gives believers who feel overlooked a reason to keep serving without keeping score, and those who are tempted by pride a reason to be afraid.

crossReferences.note: The earlier account of Mordecai reporting the plot of Bigthan and Teresh, recorded in the Book of the Chronicles. Chapter 6 opens exactly the record that was written down then, and the gap of some five years between the deed and the reading shows how patiently the book waits.

Pharaoh clothes Joseph in fine linen, gives him his ring, and has him ride in the second chariot as men call out before him. The parallel with Mordecai's parade is close, and both stories show a servant in a foreign court publicly raised after a long neglect.

After Daniel is thrown to the lions, Darius fasts and sleep flees from him. The Persian king's sleeplessness leads to the rescue of God's servant, as in Esther 6, and the parallel shows how God can use a king's unrest for His purposes.

Nebuchadnezzar's dreams trouble his spirit, and sleep escapes him, leading to Daniel's elevation. It is another example of a sleepless ruler in the hands of God, and the pattern helps the reader see the night in Esther 6 as more than luck.

Hannah sings that the LORD raises the poor from the dust and seats them among princes. The song states in general form what Esther 6 shows in one man, and it sets the reversal within God's regular way of working.

Exaltation comes neither from east nor west, but from God, who brings down one and exalts another. Haman's promotion in chapter 3 and Mordecai's honour here both fit the psalm, and the chapter shows who actually holds the power to lift people up.

Jesus says that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled and the one who humbles himself exalted. Haman's assumption that the honour is his, and Mordecai's quiet return to the gate, illustrate the saying in one scene.

Christ humbled Himself to death on a cross, and God exalted Him to the highest place. This is the pattern of Esther 6 at its deepest, and it shows that the reversal in Susa is a preview of the greater one at the resurrection.
God is not unjust and will not forget the work and love shown for His name. Mordecai's forgotten deed and the king's open book give a human picture of the God who remembers what people forget.

Pride goes before destruction and a haughty spirit before a fall. Haman's question 'whom would the king delight to honour more than me?' is the proud spirit speaking, and the fall that Zeresh predicts is close.

study.oneStory:
Esther 6 stands at the exact centre of the book, and it stands at a point in the Bible's story where the question is whether the God who made promises can still keep them. The story began with a God who spoke and made a world, and who then promised a seed to crush the serpent, Genesis 3:15. It continued with a chosen family, an enslaved people and a rescue from Egypt, Exodus 14. By the time of Esther, most of that people has been scattered by exile, the kingdom is gone, and the temple lies far away. The world's powers seem to have the last word. The sleepless night is God's answer, delivered without a word.

The chapter answers something from the very beginning of the Bible. In the garden, a proud grasp at being like God brought a fall, Genesis 3:5 and 3:7. Haman's question, 'Whom would the king delight to honour more than me?', is the same grasp in a court, and it ends in the same way, with shame and the covering of the head. The old pattern of Genesis 3 is being played out again in Susa, and this time the story shows the tempter's project undone in one day.

The chapter also sets up what is to come. It gives the story its hinge, and the reversals of chapters 7 to 9 follow from it. In the Bible's larger story, it points to the cross and resurrection. There the powers of the world thought they had marked the Righteous One for death, and by raising Him God turned their verdict over. Colossians says that He made a public spectacle of the powers, triumphing over them by the cross, Colossians 2:15.

The story ends in the new creation, where the humble are lifted and the proud have no place. Revelation shows the redeemed clothed in white and honoured before the throne, Revelation 7:9 to 14, and the promise that the one who is faithful will be given the crown of life, Revelation 2:10. The forgotten deeds of God's people will not be lost in a royal archive; they are known to the Father, and the honour they were denied on earth will be given in full. The night of Esther 6 is a small sign of that morning.

sermon.title: The Unseen Hand of God
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Esther, this message expounds Esther 6, the sleepless night and the great reversal, tracing the unseen hand of God through a chain of ordinary events. A faithful, expository handling of this movement.

quiz.q: What set the great reversal of chapter six in motion?

options.text: The king could not sleep and had the royal chronicles read, hearing of Mordecai's unrewarded deed.
options.note: Esther 6:1-3 shows an ordinary insomnia becoming the hinge of the rescue.

options.text: Mordecai petitioned the king for a reward.
options.note: Mordecai did nothing to seek honor; the king discovered the record on his own.

options.text: An angel appeared to the king in a dream.
options.note: There is no miracle or vision; the turn comes through ordinary events.

options.text: Esther reminded the king of Mordecai's loyalty.
options.note: Esther is not involved here; the king found the record himself while sleepless.

quiz.q: Why did Haman describe such lavish honors to the king?

options.text: He assumed the king meant to honor him, so he designed a parade for himself.
options.note: Esther 6:6 shows Haman's pride blinding him to the trap.

options.text: He knew the honors were meant for Mordecai and tried to limit them.
options.note: The opposite: he had no idea, and aimed high for himself.

options.text: The king ordered him to design honors for Mordecai from the start.
options.note: The king named Mordecai only after Haman had described the honors.

options.text: He was mocking the whole idea of honoring anyone.
options.note: He was in deadly earnest, expecting the glory for himself.

quiz.q: What was Haman forced to do?

options.text: To robe Mordecai and lead him through the city, proclaiming his honor.
options.note: Esther 6:10-11 records Haman's public humiliation on behalf of his enemy.

options.text: To hang Mordecai on the gallows as he had planned.
options.note: The reverse happened: he had to honor Mordecai, not hang him.

options.text: To give Mordecai half his own estate.
options.note: The honor was the royal parade, not a transfer of Haman's wealth.

options.text: To apologize to the king for his pride.
options.note: He was ordered to honor Mordecai, then went home in grief.

quiz.q: How did Haman's wife and advisers respond to his humiliation?

options.text: They foretold his fall, since he could not prevail against a Jew.
options.note: Esther 6:13 has his own household predicting his doom.

options.text: They urged him to try again to have Mordecai killed.
options.note: Earlier they urged the gallows; now they foresee his ruin instead.

options.text: They comforted him that all would soon be well.
options.note: They did the opposite, warning that he would surely fall.

options.text: They advised him to flee the kingdom at once.
options.note: They predicted his fall; then the eunuchs rushed him to the banquet.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson of this chapter's chain of coincidences?

options.text: A hidden God governs even ordinary events to exalt the faithful and humble the proud.
options.note: The piled coincidences reveal providence working through the everyday.

options.text: That good luck eventually favors patient people.
options.note: The point is providence, not luck; the timing is far too precise for chance.

options.text: That kings are easily manipulated by clever servants.
options.note: The chapter shows God overruling, not human manipulation succeeding.

options.text: That God only acts through miracles and signs.
options.note: The opposite: here God acts with no miracle at all, through ordinary means.

questions: The whole rescue turned on a king who could not sleep. Where do you need to trust that God is at work in the small, ordinary details of your life that seem like nothing?
Mordecai's good deed went unnoticed for years before it was remembered at just the right time. How does it steady you to know God does not forget faithfulness, even when no one else sees it?
Haman was so full of himself that he designed his own humiliation. Where might pride be blinding you to a trap you are walking into?
The man marked for the gallows was suddenly clothed in royal honor. How does this reversal help you trust God when your own situation looks hopeless?
Even Haman's family sensed he could not win against God's people. Where are you tempted to fear opposition that is, in truth, already doomed to fail?

translationNotes.note: Sleep escaped the king reads literally the king's sleep fled; the narrator gives no cause, and in this God-hidden book the unexplained insomnia is the very hinge of providence.
